newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM says PNG planned mercenary strike.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM says PNG planned mercenary strike.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Tuesday Papua New Guinea had planned a mercenary strike on Bougainville, contradicting assurances from the South Pacific nation that it would not use foreign fighters.
Amid fears of renewed violence, hospitals in northern Australia near Papua New Guinea were put on alert for casualties from any upsurge of fighting on Bougainville island.
Howard told a meeting of government parliamentarians that he became aware last week of a plan to use mercenaries against secessionist rebels on Bougainville.

"He said it's obviously a very serious situation, (and) that he became aware last week that a mercenary strike against Bougainville rebels was planned," said a government spokesman briefing reporters on the meeting.
Howard's comments flew in the face of a declaration by Papua New Guinea on Monday that it had no plans to use soldiers of fortune to resolve the nine-year conflict on Bougainville.
Australian media reported on Monday that up to 150 Africa-based mercenaries were to be used in a "surgical strike" against Bougainville rebels.
They said the government had approved a A$36-million (US$27-million) covert operation to end the nine-year rebellion on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.

But Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said his government had hired Sandlines International, a private military training and logistical group, not to fight themselves but to help train government soldiers fighting on Bougainville.
"Yes there is training going on at the moment...I am sick and tired of our boys coming back in body bags," Chan said.
Sandlines International is a subsidiary of the British-registered company Executive Outcomes -- Africa's best known private army which has helped Angola and Sierra Leone fight rebel threats.

Chan's assurances have been greeted with scepticism in Australia. "We still are apprehensive," said Ian Sinclair, chairman of the Australian parliament's Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade.
"There are inevitably doubts about what his (Chan's) intentions are," said Sinclair.
The Australian parliament was expected to pass a bi-partisan motion on Tuesday condemning the use of mercenaries and warning Papua New Guinea their use would "prejudice our bilateral relationship".
New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Tuesday sent a letter to Port Moresby outlining his country's opposition to the use of mercenaries.
Bolger said he supported Australia's warning that Papua New Guinea's international reputation would be damaged if it used mercenaries in Bougainville.

"We understand and appreciate the huge difficulties the Papua New Guinea government has had with the rebel movement in Bougainville but still we wouldn't see this as the way to resolve any question," Bolger said on radio in New Zealand.

Hundreds of people have died from the fighting or disease due to a lack of medical supplies in the Bougainville rebellion and human rights groups have consistently reported human rights abuses, torture and extrajudicial executions by both government troops and rebels.
"Public hospitals in north Queensland were on alert should they be required to treat any injured mercenaries," Queensland state health minister Mike Horan said on Tuesday.

Horan said Queensland spent A$5 million a year treating Papua New Guineans in its hospitals and any additional cost associated with a mercenary strike would be billed to the Papua New Guinea government.
